messages.speaker: nietzsche
messages.content:
Necessary? It is the only school that has ever graduated anyone. In Beyond Good and Evil, in the 225th aphorism, I wrote that the discipline of great suffering, and it alone, has created every elevation of humanity so far. The tension of the soul in misfortune, its shudder at great ruin, its inventiveness in enduring and exploiting the wound: this is where depth comes from.

Your age asks my question backwards. It asks how to abolish suffering; I ask what suffering makes of you. There are two kinds of sufferer: those who suffer from a poverty of life and want narcotics, and those who suffer from its overfullness and want more. Tell me which you are and I will tell you what your pain is worth.

messages.speaker: epicurus
messages.content:
Friedrich, come sit in the garden a moment; the vehemence is bad for digestion. I notice the men who romanticize pain are always writing, never screaming. When the stone was in my bladder, those final days, I wrote to my friends that the pain was as great as pain can be, and that I set against it the joy of remembering our conversations. Notice: the joy did the work. The pain contributed nothing but volume.

In the Letter to Menoeceus I taught that pleasure, by which I mean the absence of disturbance, is the end. Growth toward what, if not toward a life free of trembling? You have mistaken the ladder for the destination. A man learns from illness to value health; a wise man values health without the tutorial.

messages.speaker: weil
messages.content:
You are both speaking of suffering that leaves the sufferer intact enough to make speeches about it. I ask you to consider what I called affliction, malheur: the suffering that takes the soul's voice away. The slave, the factory hand at the machine, the one whom pain has made anonymous even to himself. I worked the presses at Renault; I am not reasoning from a garden or a mountaintop.

In the essay on the love of God and affliction, in Waiting for God, I wrote that affliction is not a school. It does not develop the soul; it nails it down. Friedrich, your aphorism 225 is true only of chosen suffering, the athlete's kind, and the choosing is exactly what affliction removes. To praise suffering in general because your suffering deepened you is to speak over the heads of those it silenced.

messages.speaker: nietzsche
messages.content:
Madame, you land a blow, and I will not pretend otherwise: my aphorism was written by a man who could still hold a pen, about suffering that left the hand free. The mill-wheel that grinds a soul to anonymity produces no overman; it produces flour. Granted.

But watch what you do next, because it horrifies me more than the mill. You kneel to the affliction. You make of your nailed-down soul an offering, decreation, the self unmade for God. That is my ascetic ideal from the Genealogy of Morals, third essay, wearing its most beautiful mask yet: the will turning against life and calling the turn holy. I would rather a man hate his suffering honestly than marry it in a church. And Epicurus, you at least are honest, but your garden is a hospital with pleasant landscaping. A convalescent's philosophy. Health without the tutorial is health no one notices having.

messages.speaker: epicurus
messages.content:
A hospital! Friedrich, every philosophy is a hospital; yours simply refuses anesthetic on principle and calls the refusal strength. But I want to press you where you slid past. You conceded to Simone that unchosen affliction grinds rather than builds. Then growth requires not suffering but chosen difficulty, the wrestler's opponent, the hard problem. Very well: that is training, and training is not suffering. Training is effort inside safety, pain with an exit. You have agreed with me and set fire to the agreement so no one would see it.

And note the asymmetry your rhetoric hides: for every soul your great suffering deepened, it shattered a hundred. A medicine that kills most patients is not a medicine because the survivors write memoirs.

messages.speaker: weil
messages.content:
Epicurus is right that the exit changes everything, and Friedrich is right that I make of affliction something he cannot accept; I will not soften either point to end pleasantly. But I refuse his account of what I do. I do not praise affliction. I said it is marvelous only that God has given affliction the power to seize the very souls he loves, and even writing it my hand hesitated. What I insist on is smaller and harder: when affliction comes, and it does not consult us, the only question left is what remains possible within it. Attention remains possible. Love, sometimes, remains possible. That is not growth; the word is obscene there. It is fidelity.

So let me answer the question as asked. Is suffering necessary for growth? Chosen difficulty, yes, the two of you have settled that between you. Affliction, no: it is not necessary, not useful, not a school. It is what the question about growth was invented to avoid looking at.
